images.title: Quarters that make 2
images.purpose: Show that a decimal times a natural number can give a natural number: 8 pieces of 0.25 fill exactly 2 wholes.
images.composition: Left half: 8 small loose square pieces; right half: 2 whole squares each split into 4 parts; an equals sign between them and one equation line below.
exact_structure: Left group: exactly 8 identical small amber #E69F00 squares with #2B2B2B outlines, arranged in 2 rows of 4 with small gaps; a grey #6B7280 brace under them with the text "8 pieces of 0.25".
One large grey #6B7280 equals sign in the centre.

Right group: exactly 2 large unit squares side by side, each the size of 4 small pieces, each divided by thin grey #6B7280 lines into 2 by 2 = 4 equal parts, all 8 parts filled amber #E69F00, with a thick green #009E73 outline around each whole square.
Under the right group, one green #009E73 label "2 wholes".
Below everything, two centred equation lines: "0.25 × 8 = 200/100 = 2" on the first line and "2.5 × 0.4 = 100/100 = 1" on the second line.
No other shapes, no other numbers.
rejection: any count of small pieces other than 8, or any count of whole squares other than 2
a whole square split into anything other than 4 equal parts
the equations showing any result other than 2 and 1
images.takeaway: A product of decimals can be a natural number: 0.25 × 8 = 2 and 2.5 × 0.4 = 1.
images.description: Eight amber quarter pieces on the left equal two whole squares on the right, each made of four quarters, with the equations 0.25 × 8 = 200/100 = 2 and 2.5 × 0.4 = 100/100 = 1.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text that asks whether a product of decimals can be a natural number.
images.teaching_notes: Count the 8 quarters and see them fill 2 wholes exactly, with nothing left over.

image_decisions.why: Seeing quarters fill whole squares makes it believable that a decimal product can be a whole number.
